items.title: Why braces inside a value stay as plain text
items.body:
Since the S13 fix, rendering is a single pass. The template is tokenized once, each reference is resolved, and the results are joined. A resolved value is never tokenized again, so a cell containing `{{connection.token}}` ends up in the output as those exact characters. The code comment explains the old bug: the renderer used to loop and re-expand references found inside values, which let a spreadsheet row pull a live secret into an action input.

- Expanding nested references is the exfiltration bug that was fixed.
- Stripping braces is wrong: the value is copied unchanged.
- An error is wrong: values may contain any text; only the template itself is parsed.

excerpts.quote: // SINGLE PASS (S13, flaw #1 fix). Resolved values are INERT DATA — we never re-scan them for more // templates. The old code looped, re-expanding any `{{…}}` that appeared inside a resolved value; a // SheetLite row containing `{{connection.token}}` would then get re-evaluated into an action input, // exfiltrating a live secret. The invariant now: user *data* flowing through the renderer stays data.
- ⚠️ A rendering subtlety around resolved values that themselves contain `{{…}}` is exactly the kind of edge the S13 fuzzer exists to find. Smallness limits the blast radius even of our own mistakes.

items.title: Why a missing path throws instead of rendering blank
items.body:
`resolvePath` walks the path one segment at a time. `trigger` exists, but `trigger.email` is `undefined`, so it throws `ExprRenderError` with a message naming the missing segment. ADR-0006 chose this deliberately: a mapping that points at nothing is a bug the author should see, not a blank that quietly corrupts the run.

- An empty string is the silent behaviour the ADR rejects; `stringify` only produces "" for values that exist but are null.
- Returning undefined is wrong: the check `cur === undefined` throws first.
- The raw text is wrong: references are never passed through unresolved.

excerpts.quote: export function resolvePath(path: string[], scope: Scope): unknown { let cur: unknown = scope; for (const seg of path) { if (cur === null || cur === undefined || typeof cur !== "object") { throw new ExprRenderError(`cannot resolve "${path.join(".")}": "${seg}" is not on an object`); } cur = (cur as Record<string, unknown>)[seg]; if (cur === undefined) throw new ExprRenderError(`cannot resolve "${path.join(".")}": missing "${seg}"`); } return cur; }
- **A missing path is a render-time error**, not a silent empty string.

items.title: Why bulk work gets a turn after five high picks
items.body:
`pickLane` checks the reserved minimum before the priority order. Bulk has 2 runs waiting and `consecutiveHighPicks` is 5, which meets the default `starvationLimit` of 5, so it returns "bulk". Otherwise it would walk interactive, scheduled, bulk and return the first lane with work. ADR-0013 says no lane may fully starve.

- Interactive would be right with fewer than 5 consecutive high picks.
- Scheduled is wrong twice: it has no work, and the reserved branch returns first.
- None is wrong: an empty lane is skipped, not a reason to stop.

excerpts.quote: export function pickLane( depth: Record<Lane, number>, consecutiveHighPicks: number, starvationLimit = 5, ): Lane | null { const bulkWaiting = depth.bulk > 0; if (bulkWaiting && consecutiveHighPicks >= starvationLimit) return "bulk"; // reserved minimum for (const lane of LANE_ORDER) { if (depth[lane] > 0) return lane; } return null; }

items.title: Rotating the KEK re-wraps DEKs and leaves tokens alone
items.body:
The requirement in ADR-0004's Context is to rotate the master secret without a multi-day re-encryption of every row. Envelopes meet it: because the KEK only encrypts DEKs, rotating it means unwrapping each org's small DEK with the old KEK and wrapping it again with the new one. The token ciphertext is untouched, and a test in `packages/secrets` proves it.

- Re-encrypting every token in bulk is precisely the cost that sank the one-master-key alternative.
- Regenerating the DEKs would force every token to be re-encrypted, which is the work envelopes avoid.
- DEKs are not derived from the KEK; each is generated on the org's first secret and stored wrapped.

excerpts.quote: re-wrap each org's (tiny) DEK; token ciphertext is untouched (proven by a test).
Simpler, but rotating that key means re-encrypting every token in the system

items.title: Why the attempt cap beats Retry-After
items.body:
Order matters in `retryPolicy`. Before looking at the error kind, it checks `attempt >= MAX_ATTEMPTS` and returns `{ retry: false }`. MAX_ATTEMPTS is 4, so on attempt 4 even a RateLimited error stops, and with fail-fast semantics the run fails. Below the cap, RateLimited would wait `error.retryAfterMs`, falling back to backoff only when there is no Retry-After.

- "Rate limits always retry" ignores the cap, which ADR-0007 says bounds all retries.
- 8000 ms is backoff(4) = 1000 x 2^3, but the cap check (executor.ts:26) returns retry: false before any delay is computed.
- 30000 ms is the backoff ceiling, not a final retry.

excerpts.quote: export function retryPolicy(error: unknown, attempt: number): RetryDecision { if (!(error instanceof ConnectorError)) return { retry: false, delayMs: 0 }; if (attempt >= MAX_ATTEMPTS) return { retry: false, delayMs: 0 }; switch (error.kind) { case "RateLimited": return { retry: true, delayMs: error.retryAfterMs ?? backoff(attempt) };

items.title: The job is a pointer; the Run row comes first
items.body:
ADR-0002 splits the two jobs a queue tempts you to merge. Postgres holds the truth (`Run`, `StepRun` and the `RunEvent` log); Redis holds only work. The BullMQ job's payload is just the run id, a pointer that says "go execute run X", and the Run row is written before the job is enqueued. A lost job therefore leaves a recoverable pending run, and losing the whole queue never loses history.

- The full run state in Redis is the alternative the ADR rejected, because Redis is not a durable record.
- Creating the Run row when a worker claims the job reverses the ordering the ADR requires: truth first, then work.
- The job does not carry the step list, and the Run row is not deferred to the end of the run.

excerpts.quote: **Redis holds only work**: a job whose payload is a run *id*, a pointer that says
The Run row exists *before* the job is enqueued

items.title: Counting billable tasks under ADR-0014
items.body:
ADR-0014 defines a task as one successful action step and lists what is not billable: triggers, filter and condition nodes, steps in a halted branch, failed steps and retries. Its own example settles the attempts: a step that succeeds on attempt 3 is one task, not three. So this run bills exactly one task, for the action step that eventually succeeded.

- Three tasks for three attempts would charge for retries, which the ADR excludes.
- Counting the trigger and the filter would bill plumbing the user did not think of as work.
- Five tasks combines both mistakes.

excerpts.quote: **A task = one SUCCESSFUL action step.**
and **retries** (a step that succeeds on attempt 3 is one task, not three).

items.title: How an array is written into surrounding text
items.body:
This template has text before the reference, so `render` maps every token and joins them into one string. Text tokens stay as they are; each reference is resolved and passed to `stringify`. `stringify` returns "" for null or undefined, uses `JSON.stringify` for objects (arrays included), and `String` for everything else. The array becomes `["a","b"]`.

- `a,b` is what `String(["a","b"])` would give, but arrays take the JSON branch.
- "[object Object]" is the flattening bug the ADR says other platforms have.
- The array itself is only returned when the whole template is one reference.

excerpts.quote: function stringify(v: unknown): string { if (v === null || v === undefined) return ""; if (typeof v === "object") return JSON.stringify(v); return String(v); }
return tokens .map((t) => (t.kind === "text" ? t.value : stringify(resolvePath(t.path, scope)))) .join("");

items.title: Templates carry untrusted data, so the language stays tiny
items.body:
Users write templates such as `{{steps.1.output.email}}` to copy a value from one step into the next. Everything flowing through them comes from outside: webhook bodies, vendor responses, spreadsheet cells. ADR-0006 therefore calls the template language the most-attacked API in the product.

The response is to keep the grammar closed: a template is plain text plus dotted path references, resolved over a fixed scope. Read `render.ts` with four questions in mind: what comes back when the template is a single reference, what comes back when there is text around it (and how non-string values are turned into text), what happens when a path does not exist, and what happens to a resolved value that itself looks like a template.

excerpts.quote: A **hand-rolled, closed grammar**: a template is literal text interleaved with `{{ dotted.path }}` references, and nothing else. No operators, no function calls, no arithmetic, no filters. The v1 implementation is a tokenizer + a path resolver over a fixed scope (`trigger`, `steps`). Two rules:

readMore.why: The whole renderer, about fifty lines.

items.title: Why a lone reference keeps its type
items.body:
`render` tokenizes the template first. When there is exactly one token and it is a reference, it returns `resolvePath(...)` directly, so `trigger.count` comes back as the number 5. ADR-0006 makes this a rule: a lone reference preserves the value's type, while any surrounding text coerces the result to a string.

- The string "5" is what you get only with surrounding text, such as "Count: {{trigger.count}}".
- The raw template text is wrong: the path exists, so it is resolved.
- An array is wrong: nothing wraps the value; it is returned as it is stored.

excerpts.quote: export function render(template: string, scope: Scope): unknown { const tokens = tokenize(template); // validates the grammar; ExprParseError on anything non-path if (tokens.length === 1 && tokens[0].kind === "ref") { return resolvePath(tokens[0].path, scope); }
- **`{{x}}` alone preserves the value's type** (a number stays a number, an array stays an array); any surrounding text coerces to a string.

items.title: Why two relays on one sheet share one cursor
items.body:
`subscriptionKey` builds `sub:connectionId:connector:triggerKey` from the binding, and the cursor key is built from it. Nothing about the relay is in the key, so every relay bound to the same resource maps to the same subscription: one poll, one cursor, fanned out to each relay. ADR-0013 calls this getting the identity right, and it closes planted flaw #3.

- One cursor per relay is the S06 design that double-polled and could fire twice on a shared row.
- Worker processes do not own cursors; the key has no worker in it.
- Nothing switched the sheet to webhooks; it is still polled.

excerpts.quote: export function subscriptionKey(binding: PollingBinding): string { return `sub:${binding.connectionId}:${binding.connector}:${binding.triggerKey}`; } /** The cursor is stored per subscription (per resource), so relays sharing a resource share one cursor. */ export function cursorKey(binding: PollingBinding): string { return `cursor:${subscriptionKey(binding)}`;

- **Shared trigger subscriptions (flaw #3 harvest).** A subscription's identity is the **resource** — `(connection, connector, trigger)` — never the relay. Re-keying the cursor to the resource means one poll, one cursor, fanned out to every relay bound to it. Getting the identity right dissolves the duplication.

items.title: Two key tiers: DEKs for tokens, one KEK for DEKs
items.body:
Envelope encryption uses two tiers of keys. Each org gets a DEK that encrypts that org's OAuth tokens with AES-256-GCM. The KEK is the single master secret, and it only ever encrypts DEKs. Each DEK is stored wrapped by the KEK, while the KEK itself lives in memory or a KMS and never in the database. That is why a database dump alone yields nothing usable: wrapped DEKs and ciphertext, with no key to open them.

- Encrypting tokens directly with the master key is the rejected single-key design.
- Storing the KEK next to the wrapped DEKs would hand an attacker both halves in one dump.
- Per-connection keys were considered and rejected as more key material for marginal benefit; the tenancy boundary is the org.

excerpts.quote: a **KEK** (key encryption key), the single master secret, that only ever encrypts DEKs.
The KEK lives in memory / a KMS, **never in the database**.

items.title: Why the dedupe window is three polling intervals
items.body:
`dedupeTtlForInterval` returns `intervalMs * 3`, so a 60000 ms poll gets a 180000 ms window. ADR-0008 explains the reasoning: a late poll can surface the same item roughly one cycle later, so the window must cover that with a safety margin. The `Deduper` evicts keys after their expiry, which keeps memory bounded.

- One interval is too short: a straggler from a late poll would slip through.
- Two intervals is not what the code computes; the factor is 3.
- Keeping keys forever is the unbounded seen-set the ADR rejects as a memory leak.

excerpts.quote: /** Window = interval × safety factor: a late poll can re-surface an item roughly one cycle later. */ export function dedupeTtlForInterval(intervalMs: number): number { return intervalMs * 3; }

- **The engine enforces dedupe.** A `Deduper` with a TTL window records seen keys; a repeat within the window doesn't fire. The window is `interval × safety factor`, because a late poll can re-surface an item roughly one cycle later. Dedupe state is bounded (TTL eviction) — it must never grow forever.

items.title: Failures, duplicates and overload are handled by explicit policy
items.body:
Three ADRs turn messy failure into small, reviewable rules.

Retries depend on the kind of error, from a closed list of error classes, so one table covers every vendor instead of each connector inventing its own. ADR-0008 is about duplicate trigger events: read it and `dedupe.ts` and note who supplies the identity of an event and how long the engine remembers it. ADR-0013 is about overload: read the scheduler functions and note what each one compares when it chooses the next tenant or lane.

ADR-0016 adds the last piece: a timeout alone is not a policy, so decide what the timeout leads to. While reading, write down for each mechanism what state it keeps, when that state resets, and which number (a cap, a window, a threshold) controls it.

excerpts.quote: - **Per-connector retry logic.** Each connector decides its own retries. Flexible, but you get N inconsistent implementations, and the engine can't reason about or bound total work. The closed taxonomy (S3) exists precisely so this policy can live in one place.
A wall-clock timeout is necessary but not sufficient — the interesting question is what the timeout leads *to*.

readMore.why: Weighted fair queuing and priority lanes.
The circuit breaker and stuck-run check.

items.title: Why connectors are data, not functions
items.body:
A connector written as a free function is maximally flexible, but the platform can only run it. A declarative definition can be described: the registry can introspect it to generate forms, validate it against build-time invariants, and version its interface cleanly. ADR-0005 puts it in one line: code-as-plugin can only be executed; data-as-plugin can be described. The zod schemas on each action do triple duty as runtime validation, UI form generation and docs.

- Speed is not the argument, and nothing is compiled to code.
- Declarative connectors still reach the network only through `ctx.http`.
- The zod schemas are required, not inferred; they are what makes forms and validation possible.

excerpts.quote: introspect it (no auto-generated forms), can't validate it (no build-time invariants), can't version its interface cleanly. Code-as-plugin can only be *executed*; data-as-plugin can be *described*.

items.title: The gap ADR-0002 admits in the S01 engine
items.body:
ADR-0002 decides where truth lives and sets an ordering rule: create the Run first, then enqueue the work. It is also honest about what it does not yet fix. The naive S01 engine persists run results only at the end of execution, not incrementally, so a crash in the middle strands the run and can fire side effects twice. Making the truth durable step by step is S07's job, and `worker.ts` carries a warning comment on the hole.

- Enqueuing before creating the Run row is the opposite of the ordering the ADR prescribes.
- Saving after each step is the later S07 design, not what S01 does.
- Results are never kept in Redis; Redis holds only the run-id job.

excerpts.quote: The naive S01 engine still persists run results *at the end* of execution, not incrementally — a real gap (a crash mid-run strands the run and can double-fire side effects).
truth first (create the Run), then work (enqueue).

items.title: Why the run cannot live in Redis
items.body:
The job-is-the-run design had real advantages: it is fast, it is one system, and there is no join between the queue and the record. ADR-0002 still rejects it, because a run is a business record that users, support and billing come back to days later. Redis is a conveyor, not a filing cabinet: it is memory-first and eviction-prone, so a flush or an eviction would erase run history.

- Speed was never the objection; the ADR lists "fast" as a point in Redis's favour.
- The missing join is also listed as an advantage of that option, not a cost.
- Losing only queued work describes the accepted design, where Postgres keeps the runs. With run state in Redis, a flush takes the history with it.

excerpts.quote: But Redis is a conveyor, not a filing cabinet: it's memory-first, eviction-prone, and its
A flush or eviction would erase run history — unacceptable.

items.title: A missing idempotency strategy stops the connector at boot
items.body:
ADR-0005 makes the idempotency strategy a required field of every action: `vendorKey`, `naturalKey` or `dedupeWindow`. The registry enforces it when it loads connectors, so an action without one fails registration at boot and the connector never becomes available. The ADR treats "optional idempotency" as a duplicate-charge incident waiting for S07's retries, and calls enforcement at registration cheap insurance.

- Waiting for the first retry is too late: the side effect would already have fired twice.
- Relay publish validation checks graphs, not connector declarations.
- The vendor is not the gatekeeper; many vendors offer no idempotency at all.

excerpts.quote: An action without one fails registry registration at boot.
Making it mandatory (enforced at registration) is cheap insurance.

items.title: Start here: an automation engine taught through its ADRs
items.body:
Relay is a Zapier-style automation platform: a trigger notices something in one service, and a chain of steps calls other services. Each sprint is an annotated pull request, and the lasting reasoning lives in `docs/adr/`.

This quest uses five ADRs, best read in this order: 0006 (the template language that maps data between steps), 0007 (what happens when a step fails), 0008 (how a trigger avoids firing twice), 0013 (sharing vendor rate limits and worker time fairly) and 0016 (what to do with a step that never returns).

Each ADR names its code in a Links section. The engine logic is written as small pure functions and classes, so you can trace them on paper. Do that for each quiz-style question you can think of before checking the answers.

excerpts.quote: Field mapping needs a way to write `{{steps.1.output.email}}` into an action's inputs. This string language is, by usage, **the product's most-attacked API**: users constantly paste untrusted data (webhook payloads, vendor responses) through templates. Whatever we build here, an attacker will feed it hostile input a million times a day.

The classic automation-engine outage: a vendor hangs (not an error — a socket that never responds), so steps wait *forever*, workers fill with stuck runs, and one bad vendor takes down everyone's automations. A wall-clock timeout is necessary but not sufficient — the interesting question is what the timeout leads *to*.

readMore.why: How the course expects you to read each sprint.
How connectors plug into the engine.

items.title: Why the connector defines what "the same item" means
items.body:
Every `TriggerDef` must provide `dedupeKey: (item) => string`, and the registry throws at boot when a trigger lacks one. Only the connector knows the vendor's notion of identity: a row id, an email message-id, a chat `ts`, or a content-hash fallback. The engine's `Deduper` then enforces it with a TTL window.

- Hashing the whole payload is the rejected engine-owned option: different events can collide and the same item can hash differently when the vendor changes a field.
- Leaving it to the user is the "no dedupe" option the ADR calls unacceptable.
- A vendor repeat header is not the mechanism: ADR-0008 notes identity is vendor-specific and some vendors offer nothing, so each connector supplies the key.

excerpts.quote: if (typeof trigger.dedupeKey !== "function") { throw new Error(`connector "${def.key}" trigger "${trigger.key}" is missing its dedupeKey`);

- **Engine-owned identity (a generic dedupe key, e.g. hash the whole payload).** Simple, but wrong: two genuinely different events can hash-collide on irrelevant fields, and the same logical item can hash differently across polls (a field the vendor mutates). Identity is domain knowledge; only the connector has it.

items.title: Why Relay does not bill every attempt
items.body:
Metering every attempt has a real argument for it: it matches the vendor load Relay actually incurs. ADR-0014 rejects it anyway, because it charges customers for the platform's own unreliability. A step that failed twice while the vendor was down and then succeeded would bill three times, and customers can neither predict nor control that. Relay absorbs the retry and failure cost as a deliberate margin decision, in exchange for bills customers can reason about.

- It would not undercount vendor load; it would count all of it.
- Billing filters and triggers is a different rejected option, metering every step.
- Hard-pausing without warning is the separate quota alternative; the chosen quota warns at 80%.

excerpts.quote: But it charges customers for *our* unreliability — a step that failed twice because the vendor was down, then succeeded, would bill 3×.

items.title: Why the mock vendors disagree with each other on purpose
items.body:
ADR-0003's vendor farm has three mock services (MailPost, SheetLite, ChatBox) that deliberately disagree: different auth headers, different pagination, different error shapes, one of which reports failure inside an HTTP 200. That inconsistency is the point. It is what real vendors are like, and it forces the Sprint 3 connector SDK to be a real abstraction. One generic mock with a uniform API would hide the very problem the course exists to teach, and would make the SDK look like pointless indirection.

- Three mocks are not cheaper; the ADR lists maintaining three fake APIs as a real cost.
- Real vendor sandboxes cannot be driven into specific failure modes, so they cannot replace the farm.
- A tidy mock makes the SDK look unnecessary, not hard to build.

excerpts.quote: Easy, but it would *hide* the exact problem the course exists to teach: absorbing vendor inconsistency. A tidy mock makes the connector SDK look like pointless indirection.
This is realism, and it's what forces the Sprint 3 connector SDK to be a real abstraction rather than a wrapper over one tidy API.

items.title: Conditions as data, with no eval surface
items.body:
Branch conditions in ADR-0010 are built with a structured rule builder: a field, an operator and a value, authored as data. That data compiles to a tiny boolean AST, so the engine gains comparisons and and/or/not without ever evaluating user-written logic. Each new operator is a deliberate, logged addition. The ADR's slogan is to give users structure and keep one execution path.

- User-typed logic strings were rejected as an injection surface inside Relay's own evaluator; the code sandbox is for code steps, not conditions.
- A mini expression language is the same rejected option, and the template renderer only resolves paths.
- Nothing is compiled to JavaScript; the AST is interpreted by one evaluator.

excerpts.quote: Conditions are a **structured rule builder** (field / op / value), authored as data, that compiles to a tiny boolean AST
user-authored logic in *our* evaluator — an injection surface and a debuggability problem.

items.title: Computing the VendorDown backoff for attempt 3
items.body:
`retryPolicy` first checks the attempt cap: 3 is below `MAX_ATTEMPTS` (4), so it continues. VendorDown is a transient class, so it retries with `backoff(attempt)`. The formula is `min(30_000, 1000 * 2 ** (attempt - 1))`; for attempt 3 that is 1000 x 4 = 4000 ms.

- 8000 ms forgets the `- 1` in the exponent.
- 3000 ms is linear backoff, which this code does not use.
- No retry is wrong: VendorDown is one of the two retryable classes in ADR-0007; AuthFailed and BadInput are the ones that never retry.

excerpts.quote: export const MAX_ATTEMPTS = 4; function backoff(attempt: number): number { return Math.min(30_000, 1000 * 2 ** (attempt - 1)); }
case "VendorDown": return { retry: true, delayMs: backoff(attempt) };

items.title: Why offloading starts at a threshold
items.body:
ADR-0012 moves a step's output bytes to object storage only when they exceed a threshold (64 KB by default); the `StepRun` row keeps a small `outputRef`. That fixes planted flaw #2, blobs bloating the OLTP runs table. Offloading every output was rejected because every read would then become a network fetch, even for tiny outputs, which is slow and needlessly complex. Below the threshold the common case stays a plain column read.

- Small outputs are not dropped; they stay in the row and are read normally.
- Postgres did store large JSONB inline; that is exactly how flaw #2 bloated the table.
- Redis holds only work, never step outputs.

excerpts.quote: Every read becomes a network fetch, even for tiny outputs — slow and needlessly complex. The threshold keeps the common (small) case a plain column read.
Above a size threshold (default 64 KB), a step's output bytes go to **object storage** and only a small `outputRef` stays in the `StepRun` row.

items.title: The recursive DFS stays as a failing oracle
items.body:
ADR-0010 executes a relay graph in Kahn's topological order: each node runs exactly once, and a node that never reaches in-degree 0 exposes a cycle as a side effect. The learner's first version, a recursive DFS with no visited set, was not deleted. It is kept in `dag-exec.test.ts` as the failing oracle, because it shows both classic graph-executor bugs: it runs a diamond's join node twice, and it loops forever on a cycle.

- It is not a fallback executor, and it has no visited set at all.
- It does not detect cycles; it loops on them.
- It plays no part in publish-time validation, which lives in the API's relay routes.

excerpts.quote: is kept as the failing oracle (`dag-exec.test.ts`): it runs a diamond's join twice and loops on cycles.
each node runs **exactly once** (fixing diamonds)

items.title: Why the graph is also checked when it is saved
items.body:
ADR-0010 validates a DAG twice. At publish, the API checks that the graph is acyclic, has a single source, is reachable, and only references upstream nodes; a cycle sent through the raw API gets a 422. At run time, the executor's `topoOrder` guards again as defense in depth. The ADR considered keeping only the run-time guard and rejected it as a bad experience: it is correct, but the user discovers the broken graph when a run hangs, not when they save.

- The run-time guard does catch cycles; that is why it is kept as the second layer.
- Kahn's order runs each join once, at either layer.
- Raw-API cycles are rejected at publish and still cannot run.

excerpts.quote: Correct but a bad experience — the user learns their graph is broken when a run hangs, not when they save.

items.title: Working out pickOrg by hand
items.body:
`pickOrg` first keeps only eligible orgs: some pending work and `inFlight < cap`. C has no pending runs, so it is out. Among A and B it picks the lowest `inFlight / weight`. A: 2 / 1 = 2. B: 4 / 4 = 1. B wins, even though it has more runs in flight, because its higher weight (plan tier) entitles it to a bigger share.

- C is wrong: an org with nothing waiting is never served.
- A is wrong: pending count does not decide; the ratio does. This is what stops one big fan-out from dominating.
- null only happens when no org is eligible.

excerpts.quote: export function pickOrg(claims: readonly OrgClaim[]): string | null { const eligible = claims.filter((c) => c.pending > 0 && c.inFlight < c.cap); if (eligible.length === 0) return null; return eligible.reduce((best, c) => c.inFlight / c.weight < best.inFlight / best.weight ? c : best, ).orgId; }

items.title: Beyond the engine core: storage, secrets, connectors, graphs and billing
items.body:
The second half of this quest reads the ADRs the first readings skipped. Together they explain where Relay keeps its records, what it tests against, how it protects the credentials it holds for other services, what every connector has to declare, how a branching relay executes, where large payloads live, how user code is sandboxed, how connectors change over time, and what the bill counts.

A good order: 0002 (run state), 0003 (the mock vendor farm), 0004 (secret storage), 0005 (declarative connectors), 0010 (DAG execution), 0012 (payload offloading) and 0014 (what a task is), then 0011 (the sandbox) and 0015 (connector versioning).

Every ADR has the same shape: Context, Decision, Alternatives considered, Consequences. Read the Alternatives as carefully as the Decision. Most questions here ask why an option lost, and the reason is always written in the ADR itself. Before reading each Decision, write down the requirement from the Context that you think will decide it, then check yourself.

excerpts.quote: Ask the load-bearing question: **if Redis were flushed right now, what must survive?**
That word is where engineering meets trust: it's a `count++` in the code and a line on an invoice a customer will scrutinize.

readMore.why: The threat model and defense layers for user code steps.
How connectors are versioned and certified.

items.title: What a failed half-open probe does to the breaker
items.body:
After the cooldown, `canRequest` moves an open breaker to "half-open" and lets one request through. If that probe fails, `onFailure` sees `state === "half-open"` and re-opens immediately, whatever the failure count, and sets `openedAt` to now. The next probe therefore waits a whole new cooldown. ADR-0016: success closes the breaker, a failed probe re-opens it.

- Staying half-open is wrong: half-open allows exactly one probe.
- Closing is wrong: only `onSuccess` closes it.
- Open for good is wrong: the cooldown always allows another probe later; no human reset exists in this code.

excerpts.quote: onFailure(): void { this.failures += 1; // A failed probe re-opens immediately; otherwise open once we cross the threshold. if (this.state === "half-open" || this.failures >= this.threshold) { this.state = "open"; this.openedAt = this.now(); } }

- **Per-connector circuit breaker.** A degraded connector trips a breaker after N failures; while open it **holds** that connector's runs briefly (instead of pounding a vendor that's already down), then allows one **half-open probe** to test recovery — success closes it, a failed probe re-opens. So one hung vendor's runs back off on *their* connector without starving healthy ones.
